sample_type.evidence_source: [007_multiple_goals_in_middle_adulthood/page/3/Text/5] We chose to focus on middle adulthood as the 'rush hour' of life (Bittman & Wajcman, 2000) when people have to manage the demands of pursuing goals in multiple life domains (i.e., work, family, leisure). During this period in life, adults are likely to experience conflicts between goals due to the limitation of resources such as time or energy (e.g., Rindfuss & Brewster, 1996). Thus, when interested in investigating if the use of SOC can help people to manage their goals when resources are limited and demands are high, middle adulthood seems particularly well suited. In a previous longitudinal study encompassing three years, Wiese et al. (2002) showed the beneficial effects of habitual SOC for young and middle-aged adults for both, the increase in work-related and general subjective well-being over time. The current study used this age group but zoomed in on the management of multiple demands in the everyday lives of middle-aged adults.
